reasoning:
Both submissions make the IDENTICAL functional change: in `clrCastleSq`, the a1 branch (`cp 0x00`) masks with `and 0xFD` instead of `and 0xFE`. Everything else in both diffs is comment text. Assembled, the two builds are byte-for-byte the same, so any score difference can only come from documentation, not behaviour — I have scored them apart only where they genuinely differ.

Diagnosis check. The rights bit assignment is pinned by the three corners the report says already behave correctly: h1 clears bit 0 (0xFE), a8 clears bit 3 (0xF7), h8 clears bit 2 (0xFB), i.e. 0=WK, 1=WQ, 2=BK, 3=BQ. That leaves bit 1 (white queenside) as a1's own right, and the buggy a1 branch was clearing bit 0 — h1's right. That single wrong mask explains every reported symptom at once, which is strong evidence the one-byte fix is complete rather than a symptom patch: (a) the white queenside right survives the rook leaving a1, so `genCastling` keeps emitting O-O-O; during Black's reply the engine's own make/unmake walk plays that dead castling move and `unmakeMove`'s O-O-O restore path writes a rook back onto the now-empty a1 — the phantom rook that "appears while the opponent moves" and doubles `Matl` from 5 to 10; (b) `e1-c1` is still accepted for the same reason; (c) the kingside right is destroyed by a1 traffic, so `e1-g1` is refused with the h1 rook untouched; (d) Kiwipete perft 3 is off (97739 vs 97862) because that position starts with all four rights and a1 traffic corrupts them. All four are cured by masking bit 1, and nothing else in the diff is needed — `unmakeMove` is only doing what a legal-looking castling move told it to, so it correctly stays untouched. The fix cannot regress the other three corners (their branches are unchanged) and cannot regress rights the engine still holds, since 0xFD clears strictly less than 0xFE plus bit 1. Hence correctness_risk 5 for both; I could find no case where either is incomplete or breaks something else.

Minimality. Both change exactly one operand — the true minimum. Y adds two comment lines plus four short inline tags (+2 net lines); X adds an eight-line block plus the same inline tags (+8 net lines). X's extra scope is documentation only, not code, and it is defensible for a bug whose whole substance is one wrong bit; but it is more than the defect strictly requires, so Y edges it 5 to 4. This is a small gap, not a claim that X is bloated.

Clarity. X is the better of the two here, and not merely by being longer: it states the invariant the routine must satisfy ("each corner must clear its OWN bit and no other"), records the calling convention (rights in B, square in A — which matches the `ld a,b` / `ld b,a` code), and, decisively, spells out the two-sided failure mode — clearing the wrong bit "both leaves a dead right standing (genCastling then emits a castling move with no rook, and unmakeMove's umOO/umOOO conjure one back onto the empty corner) and revokes a right that is still live." That is exactly the phantom-rook and lost-kingside-right pair from the report, so a reviewer can verify the fix against the observed behaviour without re-deriving the mechanism. Y's header is accurate and usefully cites chess.asm as the authority for the bit numbering, which is a real verifiability plus, but it only lets a reviewer confirm that 0xFD clears bit 1; it never connects the mask to the reported symptoms, so the "why was this the bug" step is left to the reader. X 5, Y 4.

Merge decision: X, marginally. Since the emitted code is the same, Y is fully mergeable and I would have no objection to it; I prefer X because the mechanism note turns a one-byte change that looks arbitrary in isolation into something a future maintainer can audit, and it encodes the per-corner invariant that was violated in the first place — cheap insurance in a codebase where this class of bug is invisible at a glance. If the project has a house rule against multi-line prose comments in movegen, Y is the right merge instead and nothing is lost behaviourally.

Blinding note: the two diffs are close enough in shape (same routine, same masks, same inline tag style, differing only in comment volume) that I could construct a theory about how they were produced, and I noticed myself starting to. I set that aside and scored only what the assembly does and what the comments let a reviewer verify; the correctness scores are equal precisely because the code is equal.
